newsitem.title: USA: Jobless rate no guide for Fed policy - Cleveland Fed.
newsitem.headline: Jobless rate no guide for Fed policy - Cleveland Fed.

text.p: The relationship between a low unemployment rate and inflation is so tenuous that it cannot be a useful guide for monetary policy in a low inflation environment, a senior economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland told Reuters on Tuesday.

"If a relationship exists, it is one that has no value for policy making," Cleveland Fed vice president David Altig said. He stressed that opinions expressed by Fed banks do not necessarily represent the majority view at the Federal Open Market Committee.
But the view that no causal link exists between low unemployment and inflation has gained ground at the FOMC.
The Fed has not raised the federal funds rate since February 1995 although the U.S. jobless rate continued to trend lower, averaging just under 5.2 percent in July-October.

"As evidence accumulates, people within and without the Fed do catch up with the fact we can experience periods of not only acceptable but even robust growth without significant deterioration of the inflation picture," Altig said.
One school of U.S. economists puts the non-accelerating inflationary rate of unemployment, or NAIRU, at 5-3/4 percent.

Views similar to Altig's have been expressed by Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan and Cleveland Fed economist Ben Craig, who noted the problem with NAIRU is that "correlation does not measure behavior," meaning there is no stable unemployment-inflation relationship.

Altig noted that the predictive power of so-called "regression equations" based on the unemployment rate hold only when long lags are involved and decrease when the inflation rate is low. Economic modelers use regression equations to establish if there is a relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables.

"As the rate of inflation gets lower, the variability in the rate of inflation drops, and changes in monetary policy are more limited too," said Altig. He pointed out that in retrospect, the increases that have been implemented have been fairly modest since 1994.

"The beauty with NAIRU is that you never see it. In the end, we should convince people NAIRU is not the issue," said Altig, He added that inflation's performance has been "almost extraordinarily stable," with the funds rate now 225 basis points above its level at the outset of the 1994 tightening cycle, a relatively small increase by historic standards.
Altig characterized NAIRU at the Fed as "not a discussion about the philosophical value of it, (but), the practicality of it, and I do think it's zero."
Altig said he favored a change in the central bank's mandate to the single main goal of achieving price stability.

"It would be very useful to be able to speak of monetary policy without referring to the growth rate or the unemployment rate or the capacity utilization rate, but to speak about where the central bank would like the price level to be in two or three years from now," Altig said.

Sen. Connie Mack (R-Fla) has introduced a bill in Congress, suggesting the Fed seek price stability as its sole goal. The Fed currently operates under the maximum employment/anti-inflation dual mandate.

New York Fed President William McDonough has defined price stability as a range in the core Consumer Price Index (CPI) between 0.5 percent and 2.0 percent. Year-over-year core CPI stood at 2.6 percent in September.

"We would like to see the multiyear price level target adopted by the central bank," said Altig, who is hosting a Cleveland Fed conference on the "Dynamic Effects of Monetary Policy" on Thursday and Friday.
Altig added that while setting specific price targets for the coming years may not lessen volatility in financial markets, it would help businesses in their decision-making processes.
